Ardor

/AR-der/ - rhymes with harder · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Ardor means extreme vigor, energy, enthusiasm.

No string of rained-out weekends could dampen the kite club president's ardor for flying.

Worked Example

Forty years into the trade, the violin restorer still works with the ardor of an apprentice — first to the bench, narrating each repair to anyone who will listen, mourning every scratch as if it were his own.

Ardor comes from the Latin for burning, and that is its temperature: not mild interest, not steady liking, but heat — passion that keeps its flame through setbacks. Beside it, enthusiasm sounds cheerful and weekend-sized.

How Ardor Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

passion

passion: the everyday word for strong feeling of any kind

zeal

zeal: ardor put to work — tireless effort for a cause

Antonyms

apathy

apathy: no feeling left at all

boredom

boredom: interest that has drained away

How Strong Is It? — enthusiasm → ardor → obsession

enthusiasm vs. ardor

enthusiasm vs. ardor: Enthusiasm is bright and real, but it is a milder flame than ardor — it can cool after one bad season.

obsession vs. ardor

obsession vs. ardor: Obsession goes further than ardor — ardor burns hot but leaves you whole; obsession crowds everything else out of the room.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ard

Root — ard: to burn, blaze (Latin ardere)

Suffix — -or

Suffix — -or: noun ending: a state or quality (as in valor)

Put it together

Put it together: Ard- (to burn) + -or (a state) = a state of burning. Latin ardere gave English a small family of heat: ardor is the burning itself, ardent — in this unit's reference list — describes the person aflame, and arson, fire set on purpose, glows from the same root.

Use the root in a new word: arson

Use the root in a new word: arson: Investigators ruled the warehouse fire arson after finding fuel cans stacked by the loading dock.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Ardor is heat on the page — use it for passion that burns through obstacles: ardor for a craft, a cause, a person. For everyday liking, enthusiasm or keenness will do. Its unit-mate fervent is the adjective side of the same fire (a fervent believer brings ardor to the pew), and ardent, in this unit's reference list, is ardor's own adjective.
